A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RLAIF-V and contain readable methods, experiments, figures, tables, equations, and appendices. Retained content can be matched despite substantial reorganization; no material reading gaps prevent comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, component ablations, feedback-transfer experiments, human-agreement measurements, and qualitative results in Section 3 and the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains original alignment evaluations and additionally reports best-of-N experiments, feedback-quality comparisons, and analysis of the RLHF-V dataset.

M1.justification: New Section 2.4 adds an inference procedure: sample candidate responses, score them using the length-normalized log-probability ratio between the aligned and reference models, and select the highest-scoring response. This substantially extends the method beyond preference training. Deconfounded generation, claim-based annotation, and iterative DPO remain.

E1.justification: LLaVA Bench evaluation and its Table 1 results are removed, reducing evaluation coverage from seven benchmarks to six. The training datasets, five trustworthiness benchmarks, MMStar, and RefoMB task categories remain. Best-of-N experiments reuse existing coverage rather than introduce a new domain or task.

E2.justification: v2 adds CCA-LLaVA and AMP-MEG to Table 1, VL-Feedback to the feedback-collection comparison in Table 3, and aligned-model/reference-model perplexity selectors to Figure 5. LURE disappears from Table 1 but remains in appendix Table 6. The former Self Rewarding approach remains under the 'w/o d&c' description.

E3.justification: New inference evaluations use 32 candidates for the 7B model and 16 for the 12B model in Table 1, sweep candidate counts from 1 to 64 in Figure 5, and compare selected-response lengths with and without normalization. These introduce substantial testing budgets and controls. Existing benchmark splits and stated DPO training budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds inference-scaling and length-bias analyses, feedback human-agreement comparisons, and RLHF-V composition/hallucination-profile analysis. It removes the iterative-versus-non-iterative study in v1 Figure 3, the AVG arm of Table 9, and several labeler configurations from Table 3. The two main-text qualitative cases disappear, while appendix Figures 12–13 are retained.

E5.justification: v2 adds correlation-based statistical comparisons of category-level hallucination profiles with LLaVA 1.5 in Appendix D.2/Table 11. The correlation estimator is not specified. Neither version reports repeated-training run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests; the added analysis does not establish additional repeated runs.

E6.justification: Table 1 substantially revises reported results: RLAIF-V 7B Object HalBench/MHumanEval response hallucination rates change from 8.5/37.7% to 10.5/44.5%, and 12B rates from 3.3/29.5% to 4.5/35.6%. Base-model scores and RefoMB tables also change, and BoN results are added. The PDFs do not sufficiently explain the existing-score revisions to interpret them as controlled performance gains or losses.

T1.justification: Section 2.4 introduces the formal length-normalized reward definition and its token-level formulation. Appendix C.1 removes the AVG combination formula while retaining rejection-based scoring. These are limited mathematical changes; no theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion expand the central contribution to inference-time self-feedback and reward generalization across models. The third listed contribution changes from iterative alignment to self-feedback with length normalization. Open-source feedback, self-alignment, and superior trustworthiness relative to GPT-4V remain central claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds an explanation for RLHF-V's weaker transfer based on missing LLaVA 1.5 responses and mismatched hallucination profiles. It also explains short-response bias in DPO rewards and interprets normalization as limiting information loss. These extend the interpretation, while the stated limitations concerning training cost and residual hallucination remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents filtering overly short preferred responses to keep average pair-length differences below one word, annotator English qualifications, and BoN candidate budgets. It adds direct dataset/model links. Release wording changes from 'are released' to 'will be released'; actual availability and whether newly disclosed filtering was already used in v1 cannot be established from the PDFs.

R1.justification: v2 substantially repositions the work around underused DPO rewards and inference-time scaling, adding relevant citations including Snell et al., OpenAI o1, and From r to Q*. Iterative training is now explicitly attributed to Guo et al. Additional positioning covers BPO, AMP, and CCA-LLaVA; these exceed bibliographic or placement changes.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and contribution narrative are substantially rewritten. The former analysis section becomes separate Ablation Study and Analysis sections, the main Case Study section is removed, and Related Works is introduced in the main text alongside the retained extended appendix. A new dataset-analysis appendix reorganizes subsequent sections.

P2.justification: The document changes largely from single-column to two-column layout. Figure 2 is redesigned with an inference branch; major result tables gain new rows and revised structures. v1 Figure 4 is redisplayed as separate v2 Figures 3–4, while the iterative-comparison figure, main qualitative figure, and Algorithm 1 are removed and an inference-scaling figure is added.

improvement.justification: v2 supports a useful inference extension with perplexity-selector comparisons and a length-normalization check, adds implementation information, and makes headline hallucination-reduction percentages consistent with Table 1. These improve the paper's utility and clarity. Removal of the controlled iterative-alignment study and LLaVA Bench evaluation limits the net gain; revised scores alone do not establish improved performance or paper quality.
